title: Mercy to the worlds
hookLine: the Prophet is called a mercy to the worlds (Quran 21:107)

lines: IN THE NAME OF ALLAH, THE MERCIFUL.
cards: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." It's the first line of the Quran's opening chapter, and it stands at the head of chapter after chapter.
It's written over doorways, said before meals, whispered before a long drive. Mercy is the frame around everything that follows. And in one short verse, the Quran turns that word toward a person.
Speaking to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, it says he was sent as a mercy. Not to one town, or one people. To the worlds.

teach.h: THE VERSE: SENT AS A MERCY.
teach.b: The verse is in the twenty-first surah. God addresses the Prophet and says, in plain words: we sent you only as a mercy to the worlds. No list of victories or miracles; his purpose, in one word.
The word translated worlds is the one heard in the opening chapter: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." So this mercy is as wide as that Lordship.
Some readers take it to include all people, and some widen it further, to animals and the whole of creation.
Mercy also lives in small things.
The hadith collections keep stories of the Prophet's gentleness: patience with children who climbed on him during prayer, and the story of a person forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog.
One saying puts it simply: those who show mercy are shown mercy by the Most Merciful.
In these stories, mercy isn't a mood. It's something done, often for someone who can't repay it. And it's a pattern.
Elsewhere the Quran tells believers that in the Prophet "ye have a good example," so the verse is also an invitation: those who love him try, in their own small way, to be a mercy too.
Mercy here means meeting someone who has no claim on you, and treating them better than they've earned.

how: Muslims begin recitation of the Quran's chapters, and many everyday tasks, with the Bismillah, which names God as merciful; the verse calling the Prophet a mercy to the worlds is often quoted when speaking of his character and example.

o: a ruler, sent to govern every nation on earth
a reward, given only to those who earn it
a mercy, the Quran's word for the Prophet's purpose

games.q: mercy in the texts — tap the pairs.
p: sent as a mercy to the worlds
a person forgiven for giving water

s: the verse lists the Prophet's victories
it names his purpose in one word: a mercy to the worlds.
worlds in the verse is the same word as Lord of the Worlds
so the mercy is as wide as the Lordship in the Quran's first chapter.
in the hadith stories, mercy is mostly a feeling
it's something done, often for someone who can't repay it.

games.q: a coworker missed a deadline and it landed on you. they apologize. what would mercy look like?
o: remind them how much trouble it caused.
accept it and give them a little more patience than they've earned.
games.why: in these stories mercy means treating someone better than they've earned, with no claim on you.

practice: Think back over the last few days for a moment when someone was at your mercy, even slightly: a slow cashier, a child who spilled something, a coworker whose missed deadline landed on you.

Replay it with mercy in it, a softer word, a little more time, no sigh, and let your body rehearse the gentler version without trying to fix the past. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Raḥmatan. The Quran's word for the Prophet's purpose: sent as a mercy reaching every world, not just one town or people. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: mercy. the verse calls the Prophet raḥmatan lil-ʿālamīn, a mercy to the worlds.
